case: ASRI 2.0 Eurodrone fictional eco-design, repair, supplier dependencies and strategic resilience

cues.text: Welcome to ASRI 2.0. We will examine eco-design, critical materials and operational resilience through a fictional Eurodrone case.
Choose Create Your Own Strategic Case. The single case follows Investigate, Challenge, Check and Translate.
In Investigate, four guided examples are available. We choose Eurodrone and its critical material dependencies.
Select Eco-design and Critical Materials. ASRI loads one baseline and two alternatives for comparison.
This is a synthetic support-subsystem exercise. Nothing here describes actual Eurodrone programme performance.
We ask whether qualified repair and alternative sourcing could reduce a vulnerability during in-service support.
First, define a shared functional unit, system boundary and assessment period. Without them, comparisons can mislead.
We continue to Challenge, where operating and economic conditions drive the results.
We compare the current baseline, qualified repair and a combined option with an alternative supplier.
ASRI 2.0 has a common set of twenty-three parameters. Only those applicable to this case are activated.
Open Operational Conditions. Each input shows the three options using equivalent units.
Recovery time indicates how long each option takes without additional incidents.
The binding supply lead time reflects the wait for a component or supplier when it affects the decision.
The deadline is shared. ASRI evaluates whether each strategy could meet it given the stated risks.
Open Risks and Probabilities. The model separates technical failure from external supply disruption.
A likelihood of technical success is not a qualification certificate. Failure also carries a defined delay.
Joint-event inputs can represent failures and disruptions occurring together. We must respect feasible probability bounds.
Economic Obligations shows direct outlay, logistics and possible costs of interruption or disruption.
Expected cost depends on stated probabilities and timing. Interruption cost must not be counted twice.
Contractual Conditions handles reservations and penalties. Additional financial flows can be reviewed separately.
If a condition is irrelevant, mark it Not Applicable and record why, rather than inventing a zero.
Environmental Factors covers material demand, waste and bounded emissions for the same functional unit.
ASRI 2.0 checks inventory scope and uncertainty. Neither a lower value nor a model output is a verified life-cycle benefit.
Inputs can be linked to evidence records. Their review state is declared within this fictional exercise, not authenticated.
The dashboard compares time, deadline attainment, cost and environmental outcomes without imposing a winner.
We change the recovery time for the repair option to test how the model responds.
The calculation updates immediately, allowing us to examine sensitivity before deciding.
We restore the original value to keep the comparison consistent.
Sensitivity recalculates individual changes and identifies when a conclusion may switch. It is not a confidence interval.
Repair may reduce material demand but increase cost or miss a deadline. The model keeps adverse outcomes visible.
We move to Check to identify which conclusions are adequately supported.
Check distinguishes calculated results, supporting records and the approvals still required for real decisions.
Four review gates are completed for the training exercise. They are NOT Airbus technical or corporate approvals.
These are simulated checks. The distinction between exercise completion and real authorisation must remain visible.
The case includes fictional evidence records with owners, reviewers, dates and limitations.
Each record is organised by option and topic, covering operations, technical risks, supply, cost and environment.
The example links applicable inputs to reviewed exercise records. Reviewed here does not mean independently verified.
Both alternatives are complete for training purposes. Operational results would need authorised data and independent review.
Now we arrive at Translate, where ASRI turns a completed analysis into meaningful strategic decisions.
Translate is the heart of ASRI 2.0: the same calculated evidence becomes a decision story for each audience.
A customer needs continuity. Engineers need technical feasibility. Programme needs milestones. Leadership needs risk choices.
Changing the audience never changes the underlying model or the numbers. It changes what matters to the decision.
Environmental mechanisms and resilience outcomes must be connected by a defensible causal pathway, not a slogan.
Every positive claim retains its assumptions, evidence status and limitations, even in an executive summary.
First, consider the Defence Customer. Their concern is restoring the required capability.
For the Defence Customer, the question is whether critical service support could continue under supply disruption.
A faster component recovery is relevant, but it does not by itself establish aircraft or mission availability.
We therefore express customer value as a conditional continuity scenario, not a certified mission improvement.
This is a component-level study with fictional data. Any claim about fleet readiness needs separate observations.
Seven deeper conclusions explain the bottleneck, risks, economics, environment, alternatives, evidence and next action.
Start with the bottleneck. Which step sets the recovery time: repair, sourcing, capacity or an external disruption?
Two suppliers can still depend on the same upstream source. ASRI 2.0 can document shared route dependencies.
Joint risks and capacity constraints can change deadline attainment. These are model assumptions, not calibrated forecasts.
A resilience improvement may carry extra spending, downtime cost or commitments. The financial boundary is explicit.
Materials, waste and emissions must be measured on comparable bases, with uncertainty and adverse changes visible.
Compare qualified repair with the combined repair-and-sourcing strategy. There may be no universally best option.
The evidence section identifies user-declared records and checks. No tick box is an Airbus signature.
The conclusion should say what to test next, who must validate it and which result would change the choice.
Now choose Engineering. The same scenario becomes a technical qualification decision.
Engineering focuses on eligibility, failure modes, repair conditions and whether a route can really be qualified.
The engineering question is not just whether repair is quicker, but whether it meets the technical constraints.
Technical qualification and capacity need direct evidence. Calculated resilience alone cannot establish either.
Switch to Programme Management. Here, timing, expected cost and commitments take centre stage.
Programme Management examines deadline risk, expected outlay and contractual consequences under each option.
The same result helps assess milestone exposure, recovery time and options if conditions deteriorate.
The comparison also reveals where extra resilience carries a price premium or a contractual obligation.
Finally, choose Executive Leadership and view the broader industrial resilience argument.
Executive Leadership views the broader question: which strategic dependency is worth addressing first?
Management can see common-cause risks, single points of failure and the choices that need cross-team validation.
The proposal is a bounded next decision, with clear owners and evidence needs, rather than a claimed saving.
A second route is not necessarily independent. Show what remains exposed before claiming industrial resilience.
Leadership also sees the difference between training evidence, independent review and genuine Airbus approvals.
Four audiences. One analytical basis. Different decisions, with no changes to the underlying figures.
Now select the combined repair-and-alternative-supply option. The narrative responds to this new comparison.
This option adds another possible recovery route. Its independence, capacity and effectiveness remain assumptions.
We compare the potential continuity gain against the cost, delays and environmental consequences of that route.
This complete exercise is still hypothetical. None of the numerical benefits is a verified Airbus result.
The same seven conclusions can be produced for other cases, provided their data and assumptions are comparable.
ASRI 2.0 translates sustainability choices into continuity, risk, trade-offs and practical next decisions.
Finally, export the comparison with its assumptions and evidence references for independent review.
The PDF report includes numerical comparisons, audience-specific meaning, sources and model limitations.
The editable Markdown report supports technical review without changing the calculation.
Before any real-world use, replace synthetic assumptions with authorised sources and complete the required approvals.
A versioned JSON case archive preserves the inputs and a SHA-256 integrity check. It is not a digital signature.
ASRI 2.0 helps structure a more defensible conversation about sustainability and operational resilience.

storyline: ASRI 2.0 tutorial recorded live on the published application: Eurodrone, decision trade-offs, conditional risk, simulated reviews, seven conclusions and four audiences. No real Airbus figures or approvals.
